tagline: A short letter to a young church in the Lycus valley, insisting that Christ is supreme over all things and that believers already have everything in him.
overview:
Colossians is a letter written in Paul's name, with Timothy, to a small church in the town of Colossae in Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Paul had never visited it. The church had been planted by Epaphras, one of its own people, who had come to Paul in prison with news of the believers' faith and love and, it seems, with a worry: some teaching was circulating that promised the Colossians a fuller spiritual life through special visions, food rules, holy days, severe treatment of the body, and attention to angels and spiritual powers.

Paul's answer is not first a list of counterarguments but a portrait of Christ. In one of the great passages of the New Testament (1:15-20), Christ is the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made, the one in whom all things hold together, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, and the one through whom God reconciles all things by the blood of his cross. If all the fullness of God dwells in him bodily (2:9), then the believer who belongs to him lacks nothing. The powers have been disarmed at the cross (2:15), and rules about eating and drinking are shadows of a reality that has already arrived.

The second half of the letter shows what that means in ordinary life. Believers have been raised with Christ, so they are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways of sexual sin, greed, anger, and lying, and put on compassion, forgiveness, and love (3:1-17). The letter then addresses the household (wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters), asks for prayer, and closes with a warm list of names that ties it closely to the short letter to Philemon.
author:
The letter names Paul and Timothy as its senders (1:1), and Paul signs the closing greeting in his own hand (4:18). The early church received it as Paul's without dispute, and it was included in the earliest collections of his letters.

Since the nineteenth century many scholars have questioned that. They point to a style that differs from the letters everyone accepts as Paul's (long sentences strung together with relative clauses, and fewer of Paul's usual connecting words), to a picture of Christ as head over the cosmos and the church that goes beyond what those letters say, and to statements that believers have already been raised with Christ (2:12; 3:1), where Romans 6 speaks of resurrection as still to come. On this view a follower of Paul wrote in his name after his death, a practice known in the ancient world. Others answer that style shifts with subject and with the secretary a writer used, that the letter's theology grows out of Paul's own, and above all that the personal details match Philemon, a letter almost all scholars accept, so closely (Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, Demas) that a forger would have had to copy them with unusual care. A middle position, argued by James D. G. Dunn among others, suggests Timothy composed the letter during Paul's lifetime with Paul's approval, which would explain both the Pauline substance and the different style.
date: If Paul wrote Colossians, he wrote it from prison (4:3, 10, 18). As with Philippians, the place is debated. The traditional view places him in Rome around AD 60 to 62. Others suggest Ephesus in the mid-50s, much nearer Colossae, which would make the travel of Epaphras and Onesimus easier to explain; a few suggest Caesarea around AD 57 to 59. Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the letter usually date it in the decades after his death, often around AD 70 to 90. Tacitus records that Laodicea, Colossae's neighbor, was destroyed by an earthquake around AD 60, and the region seems to have been hit hard; the letter's silence about such a disaster has been used on both sides of the dating question.
setting:
Colossae lay in the Lycus River valley in the region of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, roughly 120 miles (190 km) east of Ephesus. Two larger cities stood a short distance away: Laodicea, about ten miles (16 km) west, and Hierapolis, a little farther to the northwest. Both are named in the letter (2:1; 4:13, 15-16). Centuries earlier Colossae had been an important town on the road through the valley, known for its wool and dyed cloth, but by Paul's day it had been overshadowed by Laodicea. The site near modern Honaz in Turkey has never been fully excavated.

The population was mixed: native Phrygians, Greeks, and a substantial Jewish community, since the Seleucid king Antiochus III had settled Jewish families in Phrygia and Lydia around 200 BC. Local religion included the worship of many gods, interest in spiritual powers and protection from them, and in the wider region a strong tradition of calling on angels. The church itself seems to have been mostly Gentile (1:21, 27; 2:13). It met in homes, very likely including that of Philemon (Philemon 2), and was cared for from a distance by Epaphras, who also labored for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:12-13).

What exactly the teaching troubling the church was, often called the Colossian heresy, is one of the most debated questions in New Testament study, because Paul only alludes to it. It involved philosophy and human tradition (2:8), the spiritual forces or elemental principles of the world (2:8, 20), food and drink laws, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths (2:16), false humility, the worship of angels, and visions (2:18), and harsh treatment of the body (2:21-23). J. B. Lightfoot in the nineteenth century saw a blend of Jewish practice with early Gnostic speculation. Others see a form of Jewish mysticism that sought visionary ascent to join the worship of angels in heaven, reading the phrase about angels that way. Clinton Arnold has argued for a local folk religion that mixed Jewish, pagan, and Christian elements and called on angels for protection. Morna Hooker asked whether there was an organized false teaching at all, suggesting Paul may be warning against general pressures from surrounding Jewish and pagan religion. Each reading explains some features better than others, and Paul's answer is the same on any of them.
purpose: Paul writes to strengthen a church he has never seen, to thank God for its faith, and to guard it from being taken captive by teaching that would add requirements or spiritual experiences to Christ as though he were not enough (2:4, 8). He wants them to know Christ as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3), to continue in him as they received him (2:6-7), and to live out their new life in their households and before outsiders. The letter also introduces Tychicus, who carried it, and commends Onesimus, usually identified with the slave on whose behalf Paul wrote to Philemon, now returning as a faithful brother (4:7-9).
story: Colossians belongs to the later part of Paul's ministry, after the travels in Acts 13 to 20, when the gospel had taken root in the cities of Asia Minor through the work of Paul and his coworkers. It is one of the four Prison Letters, with Ephesians, Philippians, and Philemon, and it is especially close to Ephesians, which shares much of its content and language. In the larger story of the Bible it shows the church, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles, learning that the Messiah of Israel is also the Lord of creation. The creation of Genesis 1 and the wisdom of Proverbs 8, through which God made the world, stand behind its portrait of Christ, and the shadows of Israel's calendar and food laws are said to point forward to him (2:17).
christ: Colossians contains some of the highest statements about Christ in the New Testament. He is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (1:15). All things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (1:16-17). “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (2:9). He is also the crucified one, who reconciled all things by the blood of his cross, canceled the record of debt against us, and disarmed the powers (1:20; 2:14-15). He is risen and seated at the right hand of God (3:1), he is the believer's life (3:4), and he will appear in glory. The church's confession that Christ is fully God and fully human, creator and redeemer, finds some of its clearest New Testament grounding here.
reading: Read Colossians as a real letter, written with a particular threat in view that its first readers knew better than we do. Because Paul only alludes to the teaching he opposes, be cautious about reconstructing it in detail; read what he says about Christ as the main thing, not as a reply to be decoded. Watch for the letter's key words: fullness and filling, wisdom and knowledge, mystery, the head and the body, and putting off and putting on. The letter moves from who Christ is (chapters 1 and 2) to how believers live (chapters 3 and 4), and the second half depends on the first. A common misreading treats the household instructions in 3:18 to 4:1 as a timeless blueprint detached from their setting, or dismisses them as simply the culture of the day; both skip the question of how Paul's phrase in the Lord reshapes each relationship.

structure.title: Greeting, thanks, and prayer
structure.summary: Paul greets the church, thanks God for their faith, love, and hope, and prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will.

structure.title: The supremacy of Christ
structure.summary: The great hymn to Christ as creator and reconciler, followed by its meaning for the Colossians, who have been reconciled if they continue in the faith.

structure.title: Paul's labor for the church
structure.summary: Paul describes his sufferings and his commission to make known the mystery, Christ in you, and his struggle for churches he has never seen.

structure.title: Complete in Christ
structure.summary: Believers are to continue in Christ, in whom the fullness of God dwells, and refuse teaching that binds them to food laws, holy days, visions, and human regulations.

structure.title: The new life
structure.summary: Raised with Christ, believers put off the old self and put on the new, live in love and thankfulness, order their households in the Lord, and pray and speak wisely.

structure.title: Messengers and greetings
structure.summary: Paul commends Tychicus and Onesimus, sends greetings from his coworkers, and closes with a greeting in his own hand.

themes.title: The supremacy of Christ
themes.body: The letter's center is Christ's preeminence over everything: creation, the powers, the church, and death. Nothing in heaven or on earth stands outside his authority, and nothing can be added to him. Every warning in the letter flows from this conviction, and so does its confidence.

themes.title: Fullness
themes.body: Words for fullness and filling run through the letter. God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in Christ (1:19; 2:9), and believers have been made complete in him (2:10). Paul prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will (1:9). The false teaching promised a fuller spiritual life; Paul answers that they already have fullness in Christ and need only to grow into it.

themes.title: Victory over the powers
themes.body: The ancient world felt surrounded by spiritual forces, rulers, and authorities. Colossians says that these were created through and for Christ (1:16) and that at the cross he disarmed them and made a public spectacle of them (2:15). Believers who have died with Christ are no longer subject to them or to regulations based on them (2:20).

themes.title: Dying and rising with Christ
themes.body: Paul describes conversion and baptism as being buried and raised with Christ (2:12). The new life that results is hidden with Christ in God and will be revealed when he appears (3:3-4). The ethical instructions of chapter 3 rest on this: put to death what belongs to the old life, because you have already died, and put on the new self, because you have already been raised.

themes.title: The new humanity
themes.body: In the renewed self, there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and in all (3:11). The church is a single body under one head, marked by compassion, forgiveness, peace, and thankful worship. The household instructions that follow apply this new identity to the most ordinary relationships.

keyChapters.why: The hymn to Christ as the image of God, creator, head of the church, and reconciler of all things (1:15-20), with Paul's prayer and his account of his ministry.
Paul's answer to the false teaching: all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, the powers were disarmed at the cross, and the rules are shadows of the reality.
The new life of those raised with Christ, marked by putting off the old self and putting on love, peace, and thankfulness, with instructions for the household.

parts.body:
Colossians is a letter. It names Paul, with Timothy, as its writers, and it was written from prison to a small church in Colossae, a town in the Lycus valley in what is now western Turkey. It has 4 chapters and can be read aloud in about fifteen minutes.

Paul had never been to Colossae. The church there was started by one of its own people, Epaphras, who had learned the gospel and carried it home. Now Epaphras has come to Paul in prison with good news about the church's faith and love, and, it seems, with a worry. Some teaching was going round that promised the believers something more: a fuller spiritual life through special visions, food rules, holy days, hard treatment of the body, and attention to angels and spiritual powers.

Paul's answer is not first an argument. It is a picture of Christ. In one of the greatest passages of the New Testament (1:15-20), Christ is “the image of the invisible God”, the one through whom and for whom everything was made, the one who holds all things together, and the one through whom God makes peace “through the blood of His cross”. “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form. And you have been made complete in Christ” (2:9-10). If you have Christ, you lack nothing.

The second half of the letter shows what that means for ordinary life. Believers have been raised with Christ, so they set their minds on things above. They put off anger, lies and greed, and put on compassion, forgiveness and love. They live it out at home, at work and toward outsiders.

The letter is short, and it is very close to Ephesians, which shares much of its content and some of its words. Colossians is the sharper of the two. It was written against a danger: that believers would think Christ was a good start, and look elsewhere for the rest.

The letter names its writers, “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother” (1:1), and Paul signs the end in his own hand: “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul” (4:18). The early church received it as Paul's without dispute, and it was in the earliest collections of his letters.

Since the 1800s many scholars have argued that a follower of Paul wrote it after his death, in Paul's name. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. The style differs from the letters nearly everyone accepts as Paul's, with long sentences strung together and fewer of Paul's usual linking words. The picture of Christ as head over the whole universe goes further than those letters. And the letter says believers have already been raised with Christ (2:12; 3:1), where Romans 6 speaks of resurrection as still to come.

Many other scholars hold that Paul wrote it. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. Style changes with subject, and with the secretary a writer used. The letter's teaching grows out of Paul's own. And the personal details match the short letter to Philemon, which almost all scholars accept as Paul's, so closely (Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, Demas) that a later writer would have had to copy them with unusual care. Some suggest a middle way: that Timothy wrote it during Paul's life, with Paul's approval.

These notes do not choose. Both views are held by careful and faithful scholars. The church has received Colossians as Scripture from the beginning, and readers on both sides agree that it carries Paul's gospel. These notes speak of the writer as Paul, as the letter does.

parts.h: Colossae, and a church Paul had never seen
parts.body:
Colossae lay in the valley of the Lycus River, in the region called Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia. It was about 190 kilometres (120 miles) east of Ephesus. Two larger cities stood close by: Laodicea, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) away, and Hierapolis, a little farther. Both are named in the letter (2:1; 4:13, 15-16). Centuries earlier Colossae had been an important town on the road through the valley, known for its wool and dyed cloth, but by Paul's day Laodicea had outgrown it. The site has never been fully dug up.

The people were a mix: Phrygians, Greeks, and a large Jewish community that had lived in the region for generations. The church itself seems to have been mostly Gentile (1:21, 27; 2:13). It met in homes, probably including the home of Philemon (Philemon 2).

Paul had not planted this church. “You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf” (1:7). Epaphras was from Colossae (4:12). Acts says that while Paul was teaching in Ephesus for two years in the mid-50s, the word of the Lord spread through the whole province of Asia (Acts 19:10). Epaphras may well have heard it then and taken it home. He also cared for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13).

So Colossians is a letter to people who had never seen Paul's face (2:1). He writes as their brother, and he writes to strengthen what Epaphras had begun.

The writer is in prison. “Remember my chains” (4:18). He sends the letter with Tychicus and with Onesimus, a man from Colossae (4:7-9), the same Onesimus the letter to Philemon is about.

If Paul wrote it, most think he wrote from Rome, where Acts says he lived under guard for two years, about AD 60 to 62 (Acts 28:30), at about the same time as Ephesians and Philemon. Some place it in an earlier imprisonment at Ephesus in the mid-50s, much nearer Colossae, which would make the trips of Epaphras and Onesimus easier. A few suggest Caesarea, about AD 57 to 59.

Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote it usually date it in the decades after his death, often between about AD 70 and 90.

The Roman historian Tacitus records that Laodicea, Colossae's neighbour, was ruined by an earthquake around AD 60. The letter says nothing about such a disaster, and that silence has been used on both sides of the question of its date. These notes do not choose.

parts.h: The teaching that troubled the church
parts.body:
Paul never names the teaching he warns against, and he never sets it out in full. He only points to parts of it. So it is wise to say only what the letter shows.

It called itself ‘philosophy’, and Paul says it rested on “human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ” (2:8). It judged people over food and drink and over “a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath” (2:16). It valued “false humility and the worship of angels” and claims about “what he has seen” in visions (2:18). It made rules: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” (2:21). It was hard on the body (2:23). And Paul's answer about circumcision (2:11) suggests that circumcision came into it too.

Scholars have tried to put these clues together in several ways, and none is certain. Some think the teaching drew mainly on Jewish practice, some on the religion of the region, some on a mix, and some doubt there was one organized teaching at all. These notes do not choose, and they do not give it a name the letter does not give it.

What is plain is what it offered, and what Paul says in reply. It offered a fuller life with God than Christ alone could give, through rules, experiences and the help of powers. Paul says that all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, that believers have been made complete in him, and that the powers were disarmed at the cross (2:9-15). The rules have “an appearance of wisdom”, but “they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh” (2:23).

Many scholars think 1:15-20 is an early Christian hymn, which Paul quotes or shapes; others think he wrote it himself. It has two halves that mirror each other.

The first is about Christ and creation. “The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (1:15-17).

The second is about Christ and the new creation. He is the head of the church, “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead” (1:18). “For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross” (1:19-20).

What does ‘firstborn over all creation’ mean? It does not mean that the Son was the first thing God made. In Israel the firstborn son was the heir, the one with first place, and God could call one who was not born first his ‘firstborn’: “I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27). And the very next verse says that all things were created in him and through him. He is not one of the created things. He is the one through whom they were made.

The church confesses this. The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as ‘begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father; by whom all things were made’. In the 300s a teacher named Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, and some have read ‘firstborn’ that way since. The church, at Nicaea in 325 and after, said plainly that this reading is outside the faith, and these notes say the same, gently and without contempt for anyone who holds it. The note on Colossians 1 says more.

Greeting, thanks and prayer (1:1-14). Paul thanks God for the Colossians' faith, love and hope, which they learned from Epaphras, and prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will.

The song of Christ and what it means for them (1:15-23). Christ over creation and over the new creation; the Colossians, once far off, now reconciled, if they hold on.

Paul's work (1:24 to 2:5). His sufferings for the church; the mystery, “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27); his struggle for churches that have never met him.

Complete in Christ (2:6-23). “Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him” (2:6). Then the warnings: do not be taken captive by empty philosophy; do not let anyone judge you over food and days; do not be disqualified by visions; do not submit to rules about touching and tasting.

The new life (3:1 to 4:6). Raised with Christ, set your minds above. Put off the old self; put on the new, and over everything, love. The household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Prayer, and wise words toward outsiders.

News and greetings (4:7-18). Tychicus and Onesimus; greetings from Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras, Luke and Demas; a word for Archippus; and Paul's own signature.

Christ over all. Everything in the letter rests on who Christ is: before all things, over all things, holding all things together, head of the church, first to rise from the dead. Nothing in heaven or on earth stands outside his rule, and nothing can be added to him.

Fullness. Words for fullness and filling run through the letter. God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in Christ (1:19; 2:9), and believers “have been made complete in Christ” (2:10). The other teaching promised more. Paul says they already have it all in Christ, and need only to grow into it.

The powers. People in that world felt surrounded by unseen powers, and many lived in fear of them. Colossians says these powers were created through Christ and for him (1:16), and that at the cross he disarmed them and led them in his victory parade (2:15).

Dying and rising with Christ. Believers have been buried with him in baptism and raised with him (2:12). Their life is “hidden with Christ in God” (3:3). So they put to death the old ways and live the new life now.

The Trinity. The letter speaks of God the Father, his beloved Son, and the Spirit (1:3, 8, 13). The church confesses one God in three persons, and Colossians, with its high words about the Son, is one of the places that confession is grounded.

Colossians does not quote the Old Testament directly the way Romans does, but Israel's Scriptures are under almost every line.

The song of Christ looks back to creation. God made human beings in his image (Genesis 1:26-27). Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15), and in him the image is being restored in his people: “the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (3:10).

It also echoes what Israel said about God's wisdom, through which he made the world: “He established the world by His wisdom” (Jeremiah 10:12). In Proverbs, Wisdom speaks of being with God at creation, “a skilled craftsman at His side” (Proverbs 8:30). Colossians says that all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ (2:3).

‘Firstborn’ is Israel's word for the heir. God called Israel “My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), and promised David's heir first place among kings (Psalm 89:27).

The circumcision ‘not performed by human hands’ (2:11) is the circumcision of the heart the law and prophets called for (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). Christ seated at God's right hand (3:1) is Psalm 110:1. And the feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths (2:16) are Israel's calendar, which Paul calls “a shadow of the things to come” (2:17): good gifts that pointed ahead to Christ.

Colossians 3:18 to 4:1 speaks to wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. It is shorter than the passage in Ephesians 5 and 6, and it should be read with the same care.

Paul speaks to the household of his day as it was. In the Roman world, writers described the household as ruled by its male head, over wife, children and slaves, and spoke to him about how to rule. Paul changes that in three ways. He speaks to the weaker members first, as people who answer to Christ. He gives the stronger members duties, not privileges: husbands, “love your wives and do not be harsh with them” (3:19); fathers, do not provoke your children; masters, “supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1). And he puts every relationship ‘in the Lord’.

Churches today read the words to wives and husbands differently. All agree that they call for love and that they give no one a licence to control or harm another. The note on Colossians 3 sets out the complementarian and egalitarian readings, as the note on Ephesians 5 does, without taking a side. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The words to slaves were misused for centuries to defend slavery. That misuse was wrong. The note on Colossians 3 says what the text said to its first hearers, and how it was turned against them.

It is not a word against the Jewish people or their Scriptures. The feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths were God's gifts to Israel. Paul calls them a shadow, not a lie, and he says the reality they pointed to has come in Israel's Messiah. Paul names three Jewish fellow workers who had been a comfort to him (4:10-11). Any reading that turns this letter into contempt for Jews has turned it upside down. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why this site rejects such readings.

It is not against the body or the good things of the world. Paul's quarrel is with rules that treat the body harshly and call it holiness (2:23). The same letter says all things were made through Christ and for him.

It is not a licence for control at home. The household passage gives no one the right to rule another by fear, and nothing in it tells anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.

It is not a reason to fear the powers. Some readers have come away from Colossians anxious about spirits and curses. The letter says the opposite: the powers were disarmed at the cross, and believers are hidden with Christ in God.

And it is not a promise of wealth or a call to put any nation first. Its riches are “the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27). Its believers set their minds on things above, where Christ is seated, and the cross belongs to no flag.

Read it in one sitting, aloud if you can. It is short, and its picture of Christ is meant to be seen whole.

Read the song of Christ (1:15-20) slowly, more than once. Everything else in the letter grows from it.

Be careful about reconstructing the teaching Paul opposed. The first readers knew it; we see only its outline. Read what Paul says about Christ as the main thing, not as a code to be cracked.

Watch for the words that come back: fullness, wisdom and knowledge, mystery, head and body, putting off and putting on, thanks.

Notice the turn at 3:1: “Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ”. The commands of chapters 3 and 4 grow out of the gifts of chapters 1 and 2.

Read it beside Ephesians and Philemon. The same messenger carried all three, and each lights up the others.

And let the letter ask you its question. Have you treated Christ as a good beginning, and gone looking for the rest somewhere else? Colossians says that in him you have been made complete.

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘The firstborn over all creation.’ Why this does not make the Son a created being, as the creeds confess.
‘If indeed you continue in your faith.’ Holding on, and what Christians say about assurance.
‘What is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions.’ Why this is no lack in the cross.
The teaching that troubled the church: what the letter shows, and why Paul answers with Christ.
Food, feasts and Sabbaths, ‘a shadow of the things to come’. How Christians keep, or do not keep, a day.
Wives and husbands. What all agree on, the two readings, and why this passage never tells anyone to stay in danger.
Slaves and masters. What the text said to its first hearers, how it was misused to defend slavery, and why that was wrong.

words.line: Greek eikōn. Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15), and believers are renewed in the image of their Creator (3:10).
The heir, the one with first place. Christ is firstborn over creation and firstborn from the dead (1:15, 18), not a created being.
Greek plērōma. All God's fullness dwells in Christ (1:19; 2:9), and believers are made complete in him (2:10).
A secret of God now made known: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27).
In that world, a whole way of life, not only argument. Paul warns against one built on human tradition (2:8).
Greek stoicheia: the elements, first lessons, or the powers some thought ruled them (2:8, 20).
Food laws and holy days are “a shadow of the things to come” (2:17); the reality is Christ.
A handwritten note of what someone owed. God cancelled it, “nailing it to the cross” (2:14).
Like changing clothes: the old self taken off, the new self put on, and over all, love (3:9-14).
The man from Colossae who brought the gospel home and now prays for the church (1:7; 4:12-13).

timeline.what: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years, and the word spreads through the province of Asia (Acts 19:10). Epaphras may have heard it then.
Paul held at Caesarea (Acts 23 to 26). A few think he wrote Colossians here.
An earthquake ruins Laodicea, Colossae's neighbour, as Tacitus records. The letter does not mention it.
Paul under guard in Rome (Acts 28:30). Most who hold that Paul wrote Colossians place it here, with Ephesians and Philemon.
When scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the letter usually date it.
The Council of Nicaea confesses the Son ‘begotten, not made’, against Arius's teaching that he was the first of God's creatures.

map.title: Colossae, the Lycus valley, and the places Paul may have written from

places.name: Colossae
places.line: A small town in the Lycus valley, where Epaphras planted the church (1:7). Paul had never been there (2:1).

places.name: Laodicea
places.line: The larger city nearby. Paul asks that this letter be read there, and the letter from Laodicea in Colossae (4:16).

places.name: Hierapolis
places.line: The third city of the valley, where Epaphras also laboured for the believers (4:13).

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The leading city of Asia, where Paul taught two years (Acts 19:10). Some think he wrote from a prison here.

places.name: Caesarea
places.line: Where Paul was held two years (Acts 23 to 26). A few think he wrote the letter here.

places.name: Rome
places.line: Where Paul lived under guard two years (Acts 28:30). Most who hold that Paul wrote the letter think he wrote here, in chains (4:18).

teaching.mapNote: Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis lay close together in the Lycus valley; tap the marks near Colossae for the other two. The letter was written from prison: most often thought Rome, by some Ephesus, by a few Caesarea.
